answer_text:
Define

\[
F(x)=\int_1^x f(t)\,dt.
\]

Then \(F'(x)=f(x)\), and the given equation becomes

\[
F'(x)-F(x)=e+(1-x)(\ln x-1).
\]

Also \(F(1)=0\).

We solve the linear ODE

\[
F'-F=e+(1-x)(\ln x-1).
\]

A particular solution is

\[
F_p(x)=-e+x\ln x-x+1,
\]

since

\[
F_p'(x)-F_p(x)=\ln x-\left(-e+x\ln x-x+1\right)
=e+(1-x)(\ln x-1).
\]

Thus

\[
F(x)=Ce^x-e+x\ln x-x+1.
\]

Using \(F(1)=0\),

\[
0=Ce-e+0-1+1=Ce-e,
\]

so \(C=1\). Hence

\[
F(x)=e^x+x\ln x-x+1-e.
\]

Therefore

\[
f(x)=F'(x)=e^x+\ln x.
\]

Now compute the improper integral:

\[
\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt
=\int_0^1 e^t\,dt+\int_0^1 \ln t\,dt.
\]

We have

\[
\int_0^1 e^t\,dt=e-1
\]

and

\[
\int_0^1 \ln t\,dt
=\left[t\ln t-t\right]_0^1
=-1.
\]

Thus

\[
\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt=e-1-1=e-2.
\]

Therefore,

\[
e-\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt=e-(e-2)=2.
\]

\[
\boxed{2}
\]
